label: Someone else
blurb: A sibling, in-law, coworker, neighbor, online contact, or anyone not listed.

intro.title: Stepping away from someone else
body: This covers the relationships that don’t fit the other paths: relatives, coworkers, classmates, neighbors, roommates, online contacts, and people in a group or community.
Many of these can’t be cut off completely. So alongside full no contact, this path covers limited contact, which is short, written, practical and unemotional.

questions.title: Who is this person to you?

options.label: A sibling, in-law, or other relative
A coworker, boss, classmate or teacher
Someone online: a friend, follower or community member
A neighbor, roommate, landlord, or someone in a group or faith community

questions.title: What is still tied together?
questions.help: Pick any that apply. It changes which steps you see.

options.label: We share friends, family or a community
We share a home or building
We share money or legal ties

expect.title: You may not be able to cut everything
expect.body: Shared work, family or housing mean some contact stays. The goal then is contact that is brief, practical and calm.

expect.title: Other people may weigh in
expect.body: Relatives, colleagues or neighbors may take sides, ask for explanations, or pass messages.

expect.title: Guilt is likely
expect.body: Other people’s expectations about family or community obligations can be loud. You don’t have to meet someone else’s standards at the expense of your wellbeing.

expect.title: Some pushback
expect.body: If you set a limit and then enforce it, expect the other person to test it.

steps.title: If you’re afraid of them
steps.summary: If this person has threatened you, followed you, or made you feel unsafe, plan before you change anything.
how: Use the Safety page, and talk to an advocate or the police about options such as a protective order.
Document dates, times and what happened.
Don’t confront them. Tell trusted people and vary your routine.

steps.title: Decide what “no contact” will mean here
steps.summary: Full no contact, or limited contact? Both are legitimate.
how: List the ways this person can reach you: phone, messages, social media, shared spaces, mutual people.
For each, decide: block it, or keep it, and under which limits.
Where contact must continue, such as work or housing, plan to keep it short, written, and about the topic.
Write the plan down.

steps.title: Write your boundary and what you’ll do if it’s crossed
steps.summary: A boundary is about what you will do, not about controlling them.
how: Be specific: what you will and won’t accept.
State the consequence in advance, such as leaving the conversation, and then follow through.
Describe how their behavior affects you rather than blaming them. It usually draws less defensiveness.
Rehearse it with someone you trust, with them playing the other person.

scripts.label: Stating a limit
scripts.text: When the conversation turns to my choices, I’m going to leave it. If it comes up again, I’ll end the call.

scripts.label: Not explaining
scripts.text: I’m not going to discuss this.

steps.title: Handle gatherings and family events
steps.summary: You can attend on your terms, or decline without a reason.
how: Decline without an explanation if you want to. It’s allowed.
If you attend, set conditions: who will be there, where, and for how long.
Bring a buffer person and your own transportation so you can leave.
Don’t be alone with them, and have an exit line ready.

scripts.label: Declining
scripts.text: Thanks for the invite. I won’t be able to make it.

scripts.label: Leaving
scripts.text: I’m going to head out now. Take care.

steps.title: If it’s an in-law or your partner’s family
steps.summary: A united front with your partner does most of the work.
how: Agree on the boundary together, privately, before anyone else hears it.
Your partner communicates it to their own family. You don’t have to relay it.
Don’t vent to other relatives. It gets back.
Expect some testing and respond the same way each time.

steps.title: When relatives take sides or carry messages
steps.summary: Be warm with the messenger and firm about the message.
how: You don’t need to explain or debate the history.
Ask people not to pass messages or updates.
If someone keeps pushing, you can step back from them as well.

scripts.label: Short and warm
scripts.text: I’m not in contact with them right now. I’d rather not get into why, and I’d love to talk about something else.

steps.title: Keep a record
steps.summary: A clear paper trail protects you, and it’s hard to dispute.
how: Note the date, time, place, what happened, and who saw it.
Save emails and messages, and keep copies where your employer’s or school’s policy allows.
Write things down soon after they happen, while you remember the details.

steps.title: Move to work-only, written communication
steps.summary: Keep contact boring, brief and in writing.
how: Reply to work questions only, and keep it short and neutral.
Use shared channels or copy a manager when appropriate.
Avoid being alone with them. Meet with others present.
The “grey rock” approach, staying calm and uninteresting, can help in the short term.

scripts.label: Redirecting
scripts.text: I’m happy to talk about the project. I’m not going to discuss anything else.

steps.title: Tell your manager or HR
steps.summary: If it’s harassment, bullying or discrimination, there are formal routes.
how: Read your workplace or school policy so you know the process.
Report in writing and keep a copy.
Ask for practical changes: a different team, schedule, seat or reporting line.
Look into an employee assistance program, a union rep, or legal aid if you need more.

steps.title: Block, mute and report
steps.summary: Online contact is the easiest to cut. Do it thoroughly.
how: Screenshot anything threatening or harassing first.
Block them everywhere, including second accounts and shared groups.
Report harassment to the platform.
Tell friends not to share information about you with them.

steps.title: Shrink what they can find
steps.summary: Make it harder for them to find you again.
how: Search yourself to see what’s public.
Remove personal details from profiles: address, phone, school, workplace, location tags.
Make accounts private and review followers, tags and tagged photos.
Turn on two-factor authentication and use unique passwords.

steps.title: If they threaten you or share your information
steps.summary: This is harassment, and it can be reported.
how: Don’t engage. Save screenshots with dates.
Report to the platform and, if there are threats, to the police.
Tell trusted people and use the Safety page.

steps.title: Neighbors, roommates and landlords
steps.summary: You often can’t move, so make the rules clear and keep it written.
how: Keep communication in writing, short and polite.
Agree house rules in writing: noise, shared spaces, guests.
Consider a community mediation service. They’re often free or low cost.
Go to the landlord or housing authority for lease issues, and to the police if it becomes harassment.

steps.title: Stepping back from a group or community
steps.summary: Leaving a group, or one person in it, can feel like leaving everyone.
how: Decide what you’ll say, or whether to say anything.
Mute or leave group chats quietly.
Find other people and places, so you’re not left with a gap.
If the group pressures or shuns you, lean on your outside support.

steps.title: Keep contact limited when you can’t end it
steps.summary: Many contacts can’t be fully cut. Make them smaller and calmer.
how: Spend time around other people, and avoid being alone with them.
Share little personal information, and keep conversations short.
Leave when conflict starts.
Don’t argue. Arguing rarely changes their mind and what you say can be used later.
Build up your support system.

steps.title: Expect your boundary to be tested
steps.summary: A limit you enforce quietly and consistently is far more effective than one you explain at length.
how: Repeat the same short response each time.
Follow through on the consequence you stated, calmly.
Their guilt-tripping belongs to them. It doesn’t mean you’re wrong.

scripts.label: Repeating yourself
scripts.text: I understand you see it differently. My answer is the same.
